headline: How Regular Citizens Are Healing Local News—and Democracy
meta_description: Jackie Jantzi and hundreds of residents are documenting local government meetings for Signal Akron, reviving community journalism and reducing political polari…
summary_short: Ordinary residents are becoming citizen journalists, covering local government meetings their communities need to know about—and it's actually working to unite people.
body:
Jackie Jantzi sits in on Akron, Ohio school board meetings every few weeks, taking notes on her laptop. She isn't a professional reporter; she's one of hundreds of city residents deployed by the news outlet Signal Akron through a program called Documenters to record what happens at local government meetings and publish free summaries online. These citizen journalists don't just stretch a newsroom of six reporters further—they create a public record where residents can follow the local decisions shaping their community. "National politics feels like you have zero power," Jantzi says. "But any sort of civic engagement, like Documenters or even getting to know your neighbors, gives you a little bit of power locally."

The decline of local news has left Americans hungrier for national political coverage, which tends to emphasize partisan conflict rather than community concerns. Research by Syracuse University's Johanna Dunaway found that communities losing newspapers saw split-ticket voting decrease by 1.9 percent—evidence that people become more polarized when local reporting disappears. In 2002, there were 40 journalists per 100,000 Americans covering local news; today that number has plummeted to 7.8. Almost 40 percent of local newspapers have closed since 2005.

Yet the solution is emerging. When the Desert Sun in southern California replaced national opinion pieces with local commentary, researchers found it slowed the sense of distance between people holding different political views. Residents responded so positively that when the paper's owner discontinued the opinion section, community members fundraised to save it—launching the Coachella Valley Journalism Foundation, now supporting regional newsrooms. Max Resnik, growing a network of 25 Documenters programs nationwide, explains what changes when people engage locally: "When people have a chance to talk about politics with nuance, to talk about how decisions affect their neighborhoods and communities, it drastically changes the types of conversations folks have about things like health care, access to food, immigration."

Local news journalists dropped from 40 to 7.8 per 100,000 Americans since 2002
Almost 40 percent of local newspapers have closed since 2005
Split-ticket voting decreased 1.9 percent in communities that lost newspapers
Network of 25 Documenters programs now active across the United States
